1. Shot title and extent.‑‑(1)
This Act may be called the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920.
(2) It extends to the whole of Pakistan except Karachi Division and
Dacca. .
COMMENTARY
Object of the Act Jurisdiction of Court.‑The
object is to seize the property of an insolvent before he can squander it and
to distribute it amongst his creditors. The jurisdiction of the Court commences
when certain acts take place which are known as acts of insolvency and which
give a right to his creditors to apply to the Court for his adjudication as an
Insolvent.2
Preliminary.‑‑The insolvency
law has two fold purpose to serve. One is to give relief to the debtor from
harassment of his creditors whose claims he is unable to meet and the other is
to prevent a scramble among the creditors to get at the assets of the debtor
promoting fraud and

History of the Act.‑‑Pakistan
has always been, in the main, an agricultural country. There never was a
necessity left in this country for a system of insolvency law and there was no
native law of insolvency in India. The present day Indian law of insolvency is
simply and solely the creation of statute. Two systems of insolvency law have
been simultaneously in vogue in India, one applicable the Presidency‑‑towns
and the other to the mofussil. The first enactment on the law of Provincial
Insolvency is to be found in the Insolvency Chapter of the Civil Procedure Code
of 1859. The provisions of that act were somewhat extended to the Civil
Procedure Codes of 1877 and 1879, but from 1877 till the enactment of Act III
of 1907 they remained in Chapter XX of the Civil Procedure Code.
When the Provincial Insolvency Act of 1907 was passed into law, the
idea of insolvency was not present in the minds of the people, hence the Act
was all unsatisfactory measure and there were many defects in it. So on the 4th
September, 1918, a Bill to amend the Provincial Insolvency Act was introduced
in the Indian Legislative Council and was passed into law as Act V of 1920.
Nature and scope of the Act.‑‑The
law of insolvency is administrative of objective law and therefore its
provisions are of a general character.4 It is a complete code and
prescribes its own period of limitation.
Applicability of the Act.‑‑Any
person who is sui juris and non compos mentis or anybody of persons called a
firm can take protection of the Act. The Act is not applicable to minors,
lunatics, juridical persons and to corporate bodies.
Construction and interpretation of the Act.‑‑English decisions.‑‑The Act is self‑contained
and as such the sections have to be interpreted by themselves, without
reference to any extraneous statute. Nor is to be affected or guided by English
decisions under the Bankruptcy (English) Acts when the provisions of the Act
are unambiguous.5 The English law does not apply in this country
despite the fact that insolvency law in general 'in this country is based on
the insolvency law of England,

4. Power of Court to decide all questions arising in insolvency.‑‑(1) Subject to the provision of this Act, the Court
shall have full power to decide all questions whether of title or priority, or
of any nature whatsoever, and whether insolving matters of law or of fact,
which may arise in any case of insolvency coming within the cognizance of the
Court, or which the Court may deem it expedient or necessary to decide for the
purpose of doing complete justice or making a complete distribution of property
in any such case.
(2) Subject to the provisions of this Act and notwithstanding
anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, every such
decision shall be final and binding for all purposes as between, on the one
hand, the debtor and the debtor's estate and, on the other hand, all claimants
against him or it and all persons claiming through or under them or any of
them.
(3) Where the Court does not deem it expedient or necessary to
decide any question of the nature referred to in sub‑section (1), but has
a reason to believe that the debtor has a saleable interest in any property,
the Court may without further inquiry sell such interest in such manner and
subject to such conditions as it may think fit.

section prescribes a procedure and therefore is retrospective. Its effect Is

Courts exercising powers in insolvency.7
Section 4 gives wide powers to the Court to decide all questions

6. Acts of
Insolvency.‑‑A debtor commits an act of
insolvency. In each of the following cases namely :‑‑
(a) if in
the Provinces and the Capital of the Federal or elsewhere, he makes a transfer
of all or substantially all his property to a third person for the benefit of
his creditors generally;
(b) if, in
the Provinces and the Capital of the Federation or elsewhere, he makes a
transfer of his property or of any part thereof, with intent to defeat or delay
his creditors;
(c) if, in
the Provinces and the Capital of the Federation or else‑where, he makes
any transfer of his property, or of any part thereof, which would, under this
or any other enactment for the time being in force, be void as a fraudulent
preference if he were adjudged an insolvent;
(d)
if, with intent to defeat or
delay his creditors,‑‑
(i) he departs or remains out of the Provinces and the
Capital of the Federation.
(ii) He departs from his dwelling‑house or usual
place of business or otherwise absents himself,
(iii) he secludes himself so as to deprive his
creditors of the means of communicating with him;
(e) if any
of his property has been sold in execution of the decree of any Court for the
payment of money;
(f) if he petitions
to be adjudged an insolvent under the provisions of this Act;
(g) if he
gives notice to any of his creditors that he has suspended, or that he is about
to suspend, payment of his debts; or
(h) if he
is imprisoned in execution of the decree of any Court for the payment of money.
Explanation.‑‑For the
purposes of this section the act of an agent may be the act of the principal.
COMMENTARY
Acts of Insolvency : Classification and
construction of.‑‑The word insolvent is not defined in the Act. It
has been defined by Section 2(8) of the Sale of Goods Act, and means a person
unable to pay or settle his just debts. Insolvency or inability to pay or
settle one's just debts may arise from various reasons over which a debtor has
no control, e.g., loss in his trade on account of fall in prices, want of
foreight, natural calamities, or it may be due to the fraudulent intention of
the debtor. An honest debtor when he finds his position insecure, places his
properties, ff any, at the disposal of a creditor or a trustee for distribution
amongst his creditors, or does some other thing for payment of the dues of his
creditors. A dishonest debtor makes a transfer of his property with or without
consideration and either misappropriates the sale proceeds or keeps the
property benami. What a man does when he could not or would not pay debts are
called his acts of insolvency. An act of Insolvency forms the cause of action
to institute insolvency proceedings, and it is on an act of insolvency that the
jurisdiction of the Insolvency Court rests. Mere transfer of assets by debtor
is not per se an act of insolvency.1 Acts of insolvency are either
voluntary or involuntary act. The involuntary acts are of a kind of by which a
creditor is able to compel a debtor to disclose his insolvent condition, e.g.
imprisonment in execution of decree, sale of any property in execution of a
decree for payment of money.2
The acts of insolvency, enumerated in Section 6 of the Provincial
Insolvency Act, can be divided into three classes, viz. (i) those which arise
from dealings by the debtor with his property; (ii) those which consist of his
personal acts or defaults; and (iii) those which arise from the condition

PETITION
7. Petition and adjudication.‑‑Subject
to the conditions specified in this Act, if a debtor commits an act of
insolvency, an insolvency petition may be presented either by a creditor or by
the debtor, and the Court may on such petition make an order (hereinafter
called an order of adjudication) adjudging him an insolvent.
Explantion.‑‑The presentation of a petition by the
debtor shall be deemed an act of insolvency within the meaning of this section,
and on such petition the Court may make an order of adjudication.
COMMENTARY
Insolvency Proceedings.‑‑The
petition for insolvency of a debtor may be presented either by a debtor or by a
creditor, as the circumstances mentioned in Sections 9 and 10 allow, in the
District Court within the jurisdiction of which the debtor ordinarily resides
or carries on business or works for gain or if he is arrested or imprisoned,
where he is in custody. And if the petition is in the proper form as prescribed
by Section 13, the Court after admitting it shall fix a date of its hearing and
vesting order under Section 20, and also order the debtor under Section 21 to
give security. If on the date fixed for hearing, the Court is satisfied that
the debtor is unable to 'pay his debts, it shall make an order of adjudication,
and if it is not satisfied with the right of the debtor or the creditor, as the
case may be, to present the petition, it shall dismiss it.
Petitioning creditor.‑‑Any
person entitled to mace proceedings at law or in equity for the recovery of a
debt may be a petitioning creditor. The expression `creditors generally' means
all the creditors and not some only.2
A partner can present an application for adjudicating a co‑partner
insolvent only in respect of a distinct debt for which an action might have
been brought notwithstanding the partnership.3

Joint petition.‑‑There is no
legal bar to a single application being made by a creditor for adjudication of
two or more persons as insolvents if they are jointly liable on a debt or have committed
a joint act of insolvency.4 The question, however, whether such an
application should be jointly tried and decided is a question of fact.5
In order to maintain a joint petition against two or more persons, it is
necessary that some act of insolvency should have been committed by each of
them. This may be a joint act. A single petition for the adjudication of
several debtors is sustainable if the debtors incurred a joint liability and
had committed certain acts of insolvency.6 A joint petition by several
debtors for adjudication as insolvents is not per se bad in law; the true test
to apply is whether a joint petition would be bad for multifariousness, that is
to say, misjoinder of causes of acti6 or of parties.7
Discretion of the Court.‑The use
of word "may" shows that the order of adjudication is in the
discretion of the Court. District when applies to law always means discretion
guided by judicial principles. It must be governed by rule and not by humour.
If the petition for the adjudication of 9 debtor as an insolvent satisfies the
provisions of the law the Court has nothing to do but to accept it.
Application to adjudicate undischarged insolvent.‑‑There is nothing, either in the Provincial Insolvency
Act or any other provisions of law, which debars either creditor or a debtor
from proceedings by a fresh application under the Provincial Insolvency act,

yet obtained an order of discharge.8

to adjustment of security. He can make claim in respect of such balance amount

committed an act of insolvency within three months of the presentation of the
petition.
Proof as to the existence of debt.‑‑Section
24 provides that the Court is to enquire as to whether the creditor is entitled
to present the petition, and Section 9 lays down among other conditions that in
order to be able to present a petition, there must be a debt due to the
creditor amounting to Rs. 500 or more. This means that the creditor must be
allowed under Section 24 to prove his debt if the debtor denies its existence.
Further Section 25 provides for dismissal of the petition on creditor's failure
to prove his right to present it, and this obviously involves the necessity of
proving that right. Therefore, the Insolvency Court is bound to make an enquiry
into the existence of debt.1
Sub‑section (2) : examination of the debtor.‑‑The procedure is designed not only to give the
Receiver and the creditor an opportunity of asking the debtor for information
on any point which they may desire, but also to disclose to the world the
manner in which he has conducted his business and managed his affairs, it is
important that any creditor who has reasons to suspect dealings by the bankrupt
which will prejudice an application for his discharge should have these
dealings investigated on public examination. The debtor's account of his
affairs is thus recorded and kept available for the use and guidance of all
concerned in the collection and realisation of the assets and in dealing with
the debtor according to his deserts. It is particularly useful to the Receiver
in dealing with the transactions of the insolvent.
The provisions of Section 24(2) are mandatory and the Court must
examine the insolvent before dismissing his petition.

For the application of the provisions of Section 26 it is not necessary that at

separate application even through it did not do so at the time of the dismissal
of the petition 7
Debtor.‑‑The word `debtor'
in this section means any person against whom an insolvency application has
been presented by a creditor.

Adjudication.‑‑‑ (1) If the Court

his discharge.

Order of adjudication.‑‑Under
the present section the Court has no other alternative but to pass either an
order of adjudication or to dismiss it. It cannot consider any scheme for
composition before adjudicatlon.2 Where the petitioner has brought
his case within the four corners of the Act he is entitled to an order of
adjudication as a matter of right when there is no question of the abuse of the
process of the Court. The order of adjudication must be unconditional and must
specify the time for discharge. Where the court does not specify such time, the
penalty prescribed by Section 43 does not come into operation.3 The
Court has no power to set aside a transfer at the time of making an order of
adjudication even if the act of insolvency on which the petition is found1d is
that very transfer 4
Adjudication on a compromise.‑‑A
proceeding. in insolvency is a proceeding in rem which binds not merely the

doubtful whether an adjudication order can be grounded entirely on a petition

is open to an Insolvency Court to extend the period specified in the order of

his power in the realisation of his property and the distribution of the
proceeds among his creditors.
(2) On the making of an order of adjudication, the whole of the
property of the insolvent shall vest in the Court or in a receiver as

is indebted in respect of any debt provable under this act shall during the

the insolvent in respect of the debt, or commence any suit or other legal

(4) All property which is acquired by or devolves on the insolvent

Sub‑section

their dues out of the same. He is bound to appear for examination though he may
reside more than two hundred miles away from the Court‑house.1
Where no receiver has been appointed and the property of insolvent
stands ested in Court the court may be substituted as respondent in suit
against insolvent.2
Secured creditor cannot claim any preferential treatment in
distribution of assets of insolvent. He has a right to realise security or to
relinquish as provided by Section 47. Order of adjudication as to insolvency
would not affect position of secured creditor as after adjudication he would be
free to deal with his security and to realise it for repayment of debt. It was
not necessary to give any preferential treatment or priority to secured
creditor in respect of debt, which remains unsatisfied after realization of
security, as right of a secured creditor has sufficiently been protected and
liberty to deal with security has been given to hirri.3

February, 1920]
29. Stay of
pending proceedings.‑‑Any Court in
which suit or other proceeding is pending against a debtor shall, on proof that
an order of adjudication has been made against him under this Act, either stay the
proceeding, or allow it to continue on such terms as such Court may impose.
COMMENTARY
Scope.‑‑Section 28(2) of the
Act provides that on adjudication of a debtor no creditor to whom he is
indebted shall during the pendency of the insolvency proceeding have any remedy
against the property of the insolvent in respect of the debt, or commence any
suit or other legal proceedings without the leave of the Court. This does not
provide for the suits that are already pending against the insolvent. In regard
to such suits it is provided by Section 29, that on proof that an order of
adjudication has been made, these suits will be stayed or allowed to be
continued on such terms as the Court will impose.4 There is nothing
in the Provincial Insolvency Act, empowering the Insolvency Court to stay
proceedings pending against the insolvent before that Court or any other Court.

proceeding was pending against the debtor to stay it or to continue It.1
In order to exercise the discretionary power Section 29, it is
incumbent upon the court to consider whether there are special circumstances to
justify the continuance of the suit. Where the insolvent is the only defendant
and the claim relates to a debt there is a greater reason to stay the suit,
since the debt is provable in insolvency. But where besides him another person
is also sued and the claim is laid in the alternative the continuance of the
suit is more desirable.2
Provisions of Section 29 cannot be invoked where the suit is filed
after adjudication.3

leave.‑‑There is a conflict of opinion
as to whether Section 29 applies to cases where suits or proceedings are
commenced without leave against the insolvent after an order of adjudication in
ingnorance of it. It has been held that the proper remedy of a person who has
instituted a suit against the insolvent without obtaining the leave of the
Insolvency Court is to apply under Section 29 to the Court in which he has
instituted the suit for leave to continue the suit against the insolvent.4

54‑A. By whom petitions
for annulment may be made.‑‑A petition for the annulment of any
transfer under section 53, or of any trnasfer, payment, obligation or judicial
proceeding under Section 54, may be made by the receiver or, with the leave of
the Court, by any creditor who has proved his debt and who satisfies the Court
that the receiver has been requested and has refused to make such petition.
COMMENTARY
Property of
debtor vests in appointee. Vesting is for benefit of general body of
creditors. Object and result of appointment under Section 37 stated.‑‑It
is the first part of Section 37(1) of the Provincial Insolvency Act which
validates the act of the Official Receiver or creditor under section 54‑A
in moving prior to the annulment, to avoid under section 53 and 54 a transfer
made by an insolvent and that the Official Receiver or creditor may continue
such an application even though there is another person in whom the property
has vested as appointee under Section 37. An appointee as such cannot continue
it because the right to avoid the trnasfer is not that of the debtor, but of
the Official Receiver or creditor and the appointment vests in the appointee
only "the property of the debtor". Upon such an application resulting
in Avoidance of any such transfer of property by the debtor, property would
become available to which the order of appointment would apply. This is an
additional reason therefore, for making an order of appointment under Section
37, for such an appointment gets in for the benefit of the general body of
creditor's property screened from them by the fraud or the debtor and
correspondeningly such an appointment prevents the debtor from gaining an
advantage from his own wrong in having made the fraudulent transfer. That would
be the result if no appointment were made under section 37 and the property of
the debtor were allowed to revert to him.1
